title: The mind as friend
hook: the mind can be enemy or friend; the Word makes it a friend

segments.voice: Yesterday: ego is not you. Haumai is fog on the mirror, not the face. Your line was not self-hatred. When you slipped, what did you say to yourself instead of the old speech? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-three.

Three in the morning, and somebody in your head is talking. The bill you forgot. The thing you said at dinner. The email you haven't answered. A list of what might go wrong tomorrow, read out loud, twice. It's like sharing a room with a roommate who never sleeps and never runs out of news. There are two usual strategies: argue with it, or try to drown it out. The Gurus try a third. In the Granth, hymns turn to that restless roommate and speak to it directly, almost tenderly. O my mind. Today's word is the roommate.
screen: `3 A.M. AND SOMEONE IS TALKING.` → `ARGUE, OR DROWN IT OUT?` → `A THIRD WAY: O MY MIND.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Man, said like mun, is the mind in the Granth: not only the thinking part, but the restless inner self that wants, fears, wanders and chooses. Second, the mind that pulls away. The Granth is honest that the man can run after everything shiny and drag a person with it. In the Japji, Guru Nanak puts it in four words, man jeetai jag jeet: win the mind, and you win the world. Some readers hear jeet as conquer; some hear it as win over, the way you'd win over a skeptical friend. Either way, the struggle is real and it is inside. Third, the mind spoken to as a friend. In Raag Asa, Guru Amar Das addresses the mind with something close to respect. In paraphrase: O my mind, you are the form of the light; recognize your own source. He doesn't call it garbage. He reminds it who it is, the way you'd remind a friend who has forgotten. Fourth, what turns an enemy into a friend. In the Granth, the answer keeps coming back to the shabad, the Guru's Word. A mind with nothing to hold grabs at everything. A mind given the Word has somewhere to rest. A bored dog chews the furniture, and lies down calm once it has a job. The Gurus don't throw the mind out of the house. They give it work. So the line between enemy and friend isn't about having a mind, or even a noisy one. It's about what the mind is given to hold. Befriend the mind.
screen: `MAN: THE RESTLESS INNER SELF.` · `WIN THE MIND, WIN THE WORLD.` · `O MIND, YOU ARE THE FORM OF LIGHT.` · `GIVE THE MIND THE WORD TO HOLD.` · then, large: `BEFRIEND THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: befriend your mind. Settle, and breathe. Let the mind do whatever it's doing. Don't fight it. When a thought arrives, greet it the way you'd greet a friend at the door: oh, it's you. Then hand your mind one thing to hold. If you pray, you can give it Waheguru, said softly on the breath. If you don't, give it the breath itself: in, and out. When it wanders, and it will, don't scold it. Just say, O my mind, come back, and hand it the word again. The bell holds the time.
Man. The mind: the restless inner self that can pull a person away or walk beside them, and that the Guru addresses as the form of light. Today's word.

Your line: befriend the mind. Today, when your mind starts racing, try speaking to it once the way the Gurus do: O my mind. Then give it one thing to hold. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib speak directly to the mind, 'O my mind', and Sikhs use the Guru's Word and repetition of the Name, such as Waheguru, to steady it.
